opus-5.5.text:
I think we're at a really exciting inflection point, but still early in the arc. If you look back a few years, the question was whether AI could make a meaningful contribution to science at all. With things like AlphaFold, I think that question has been answered pretty decisively. Predicting the structure of essentially all known proteins, and having that used by millions of researchers around the world, showed that AI can solve problems that had been open for decades, and not just as a curiosity but as a tool that changes how science gets done day to day.

What we're seeing now is a broadening. It's no longer one flagship result. Across materials discovery, mathematics, genomics, weather forecasting, fusion control, people are finding that the same ingredients apply: a well-defined problem, a good way to measure progress, and enough data or a good enough simulator. When those come together, AI can move remarkably fast.

That said, I'd describe this as the end of the beginning rather than anything close to maturity. Much of the impact so far has been in what I'd call "prediction problems": given an input, predict a structure or property. The next frontier is AI that participates more fully in the scientific process: generating hypotheses, designing experiments, reasoning across literature, and working in a loop with real laboratories. That's where large language models and agentic systems become really interesting, because they can act as a kind of collaborator rather than just a specialized tool.

There are real challenges. Verifying AI-generated insights, making sure outputs are reliable and grounded, and getting these tools into the hands of scientists in a form they trust and can use are all hard problems. Data is a bottleneck in many fields too. But my sense is that over the next decade we'll look back and see this period as the moment when the way we do science fundamentally shifted. The rate of discovery itself could accelerate, and that's a profound thing for humanity.

r001.rationale: The response describes an active transition already underway: it calls this an inflection point and says AI’s scientific impact is broadening across fields now.

r002.rationale: It does not say that being in the midst of the transition makes it difficult to recognize.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we're at a genuinely interesting inflection point, but I want to be careful about how I characterize it, because there's a lot of hype in this space.

If you look back at the last few years, the clearest success story is something like AlphaFold. Protein structure prediction was a fifty-year-old grand challenge, and we went from a world where determining a single structure could take a PhD student years to one where the structures of essentially every known protein are available to anyone with a browser. Millions of researchers have used it. That's not a demo, that's a tool that changed how an entire field does its work.

But I think it's important to understand why that worked, because it tells you where we are more broadly. AlphaFold worked because there was a well-posed problem, a clear way to measure success, and decades of high-quality experimental data in the Protein Data Bank that the community had painstakingly curated. Those three ingredients, a crisp question, a verifier, and data, are what let the method get traction.

So where are we now? I'd say we've shown that AI can be a really powerful instrument for science, in the way that the microscope or the telescope were instruments. It lets us see things we couldn't see before. We've seen that in materials discovery, in weather prediction, in genomics with things like variant effect prediction, in mathematics with systems that can find new constructions or help with proofs. What we haven't yet fully shown is AI as a genuine collaborator in the scientific process itself, something that forms hypotheses, decides what experiment to run next, interprets the result, and iterates. That loop is still mostly driven by humans.

I think that's the frontier. The large language models have given us a new capability, which is that models can now read and reason over the scientific literature in a way that wasn't possible before. Combined with the more specialized systems that can actually predict or simulate the physical world, you start to get something that looks like an end-to-end discovery engine. We're seeing early versions of that, where a system can propose ideas and some of them turn out to be genuinely novel and useful. But the hit rate is still modest, and the hard part is verification. Nature doesn't care how confident the model is. You still have to go into the lab and check.

So if I had to put a marker down, I'd say we're past the proof-of-concept phase and into the "real tools, real impact in specific domains" phase. The next phase, which I think is coming over the next several years rather than decades, is where these systems become general enough to accelerate discovery across fields, not just in the handful where the data and problem structure happened to line up nicely. And I think the biggest bottleneck there won't be the models. It'll be the experimental side, how fast we can actually test what they propose, and whether we build the infrastructure to close that loop.

r001.rationale: The response says we are past proof of concept and already in a phase of real tools and real impact in specific domains, conveying that AI-accelerated discovery is underway.

r002.rationale: The response cautions about hype but does not say that being in the midst of this transition makes it difficult to recognize.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re at a very exciting point, but still quite early. We’re seeing that AI can do more than help us analyze scientific data. It can help us tackle problems that have resisted progress for a long time, and that starts to change our sense of what might be possible.

But scientific discovery is more than producing a prediction. You need to understand whether that prediction is reliable, test it, and see whether it leads to something useful. So the opportunity is to bring AI into that whole cycle: helping scientists formulate hypotheses, design experiments, interpret results, and decide what to investigate next.

For me, the real measure of success is whether we enable scientists to ask questions they couldn’t realistically ask before. Can we make an experiment feasible that would otherwise take too much time or too many resources? Can we shorten the distance between an idea and the evidence needed to assess it? We’re beginning to see that happen, but there’s a great deal still to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI is beginning to change what is possible and that progress is still early; it does not clearly state that we are already in the midst of the era.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that the transition is difficult to recognize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re at a very exciting point where AI is starting to change how scientific discovery happens. For a long time, the question was whether these systems could help us tackle genuinely difficult scientific problems. Now the question is how broadly we can apply them, and how we connect their predictions to experiments that produce new knowledge.

What makes this so powerful is the possibility of shortening the cycle between forming a hypothesis, testing it, and learning from the result. AI can help scientists explore a much larger space of possibilities and identify which experiments are most promising. But a prediction is not the same as a discovery. You still need careful validation, and you need to understand where the system is reliable and where it isn’t.

So I would say we’re early, but we’ve moved beyond just imagining the potential. The opportunity now is to make these capabilities useful across more areas of science, working closely with the people who understand the questions and can test the answers.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is starting to change scientific discovery and that the field is still early; it does not clearly state that we are already in the midst of the era.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that being in the midst of the transition makes it difficult to recognize.
